nutshell: San Diego is a folk-dance town more than a session town, and a heritage town more than either. Balboa Park works like a city-run folk campus: international, Scottish, céilí, square, morris and Cajun dancing fill its exposition halls most nights, and the House of Pacific Relations' 38 cultural cottages stage about 55 free lawn programs a year. For a fiddler it is thin: one weekly Irish pub session (the Ould Sod, since 2000), a Comhaltas branch only since 2017, a well-organized bluegrass network, contra down to about twice a month, and no verifiable old-time jam. Its history is rich and unusually well taped: Sam Hinton, Lou Curtiss's San Diego State Folk Festival (1967-87) and Folk Arts Rare Records, the Scottsville Squirrel Barkers. Its living depth is Kumeyaay bird singing, school mariachi, danza azteca in Chicano Park, Navy-linked Filipino and Chamorro troupes, and a son jarocho fandango played through the border fence.

top_surprises: 'Waiting for Nancy', an old-time jam standard in the Portland Collection, was written in 1972 by San Diego banjo player Curt Bouterse while he waited in Old Town for a friend who never came (https://tunearch.org/wiki/Annotation:Waiting_for_Nancy).

Balboa Park is in effect a city-run folk-dance campus: about 31 modern Western square dance nights a month in central San Diego, plus weekly international, Scottish, céilí, morris and Cajun dancing in city halls, and a free Sunday folk dance open to anyone (https://www.idasdc.com/).

Fandango Fronterizo (2008) plays son jarocho through the border fence at Friendship Park. At the first one, Border Patrol asked them to wrap up, so they played 'La Bamba' for an hour; since 2018 nobody may play on the US side (https://sandiegomagazine.com/everything-sd/arts-culture/fandango-fronterizo-music-festival/).

Southwestern College in Chula Vista began the world's first college music degree with a mariachi specialization in 2004. School mariachi spread in the 1990s partly so Latino parents would come to parent-teacher nights (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/12/the-one-of-a-kind-mariachi-museum-in-chula-vista-has-lost-its-home-now-what/).

The first San Diego State Folk Festival (1967) had a $350 budget and spent $250 of it on Bill Monroe. The Library of Congress now holds 420 tapes of the 1967-75 festivals, with Tommy Jarrell, Kyle Creed, Benny Thomasson and the Balfa Brothers (https://blogs.loc.gov/folklife/2018/07/lou-curtiss-san-diego-folk-promoter-1939-2018/).

The 1970s Balboa Park Old Time Banjo and Fiddle Contests advertised bribable judges, gave bags of rutabagas as prizes, once split an award between a gospel bluegrass band and Hare Krishna chanters 'for traditional dogma', and ended only when the park stopped supplying electricity (https://sandiegotroubadour.com/fiddle-contests/).

A Navy port that is home to the Star of India has no public shanty sing; the Maritime Museum's Sea Chantey Festival (1993-2019) quietly died with COVID (https://seashanties4all.com/venues/festival-of-sail-in-san-diego/).

San Diego's best folk radio show airs on Rez Radio 91.3, founded by the Pala Band after the 2007 wildfires: Joel Rafael's 'Rockin' the Rez', 449 episodes (https://sandiegotroubadour.com/good-radio-is-out-there-you-just-have-to-know-where-to-look/).

The Comhaltas branch exists because a Cork grandfather, visiting for a christening in 2017, talked the local players into founding one; its founding board member notes she has no Irish heritage (https://www.sandiegocomhaltas.org/comhaltas-in-san-diego-california/).

Kumeyaay bird songs, which singers say were 'hanging from a thread', are now civic protocol: about a dozen bird-singing groups performed at the Safari Park on Indigenous Peoples' Day 2025 (https://www.times-advocate.com/articles/tribe-celebrates-indigenous-peoples-day-at-safari-park/).

timeline.event: Kumeyaay (Ipai-Tipai / Kumiai) homeland: Barona Cultural Center & Museum holds objects dating back as far as ~10,000 years and presents Kumeyaay bird songs in 'listening alcoves'. Bird-song cycles, peon (gambling) songs, Wildcat and Salt song cycles are the oldest documented song traditions of the county.
Mission era begins; Kumeyaay ceremonies suppressed, but allegorical bird songs survive as the remnant of many song cycles.

Mission San Diego de Alcalá founded on Kumeyaay land (first of the California missions); Kumeyaay converts were trained in Western instruments and joined mission choirs and orchestras (Wikipedia 'Kumeyaay', citing Bacich; founding per calindianmissions.org).

Richard Henry Dana (Two Years Before the Mast) works at the San Diego hide-houses alongside Hawaiian ('Kanaka') sailors and describes the improvisatore 'Mr. Mannini' singing for an hour at a time, satirizing his co-workers; elsewhere Dana notes violin and guitar as the only instruments he heard in Californio fandangos, where San Diego's Don Juan Bandini was a star dancer.

Azorean Portuguese fishing families settle on the Point Loma waterfront (La Playa, Roseville), later joined by Madeirans and Italian fishermen in Little Italy - the root of the tuna-fleet communities.
Cupeño people removed from Cupa (Warner Springs) to Pala; later commemorated by Cupa Days.

Ethnographer Constance Goddard DuBois records that Hatakek of Manzanita knew all the old Kumeyaay songs including bird songs, dances and the image-ceremony songs (cited by the Viejas Band's history pages).

T.T. Waterman (UC Berkeley) makes wax-cylinder recordings of Kumeyaay/Diegueño speakers and songs (1907-1909), now in the Phoebe A. Hearst Museum of Anthropology; Waterman published 'The Religious Practices of the Diegueño Indians' in 1910.
First Festa do Espírito Santo celebrated by Point Loma Portuguese families.

Point Loma's Portuguese community holds its first Festa do Espírito Santo (Holy Spirit festa) - often called San Diego's oldest ethnic festival; still held each spring with a procession and free sopas.

Panama-California Exposition in Balboa Park: the 'Painted Desert' exhibit housed Hopi, Zuni and other Pueblo people who performed dances on site; the Exposition's anthropology exhibit became the San Diego Museum of Man (now Museum of Us), which today exhibits Kumeyaay culture.
Original Portuguese Hall and capela built in Point Loma (current hall 1948).
Buddhist Temple of San Diego founded (centennial in 2026).

Bostonia Ballroom opens east of El Cajon (Lou Curtiss gives 'early 30s' or '1929 or so'); big bands in the 1930s, then from the 1940s the county's country-music showcase (Bob Wills, Spade Cooley, Ernest Tubb, Lefty Frizzell, Johnny Cash, Maddox Brothers and Rose; local owner-bandleader Smokey Rogers).

A widely circulated flyer invites the public to a large annual Kumeyaay fiesta at Capitan Grande; multi-day reservation fiestas with old dances were a public face of Kumeyaay music in the early 20th century.
House of Pacific Relations international cottages built for the California Pacific International Exposition.
House of Ireland founded in Balboa Park for the California Pacific International Exposition; it later hosts weekend sessions and Comhaltas.

WPA California Folk Music Project (Sidney Robertson Cowell, 1938-40) records 35 hours in 12 languages, mostly in Northern California; a search of the LOC online collection returns zero San Diego items - no evidence the project recorded in San Diego County.
Lalo Guerrero works at Convair in San Diego during WWII and entertains at military camps.
Sam Hinton (b. Tulsa 1917) moves to San Diego to work at the UC Division of War Research on Point Loma; from 1946 to 1964 he is curator of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography aquarium-museum.
Sam Hinton moves to San Diego (UC Division of War Research, Point Loma); curates the Scripps aquarium 1946-64.
Sam Hinton records 56 songs for the Library of Congress (issued 1999 by Bear Family as 'The Library of Congress Recordings').
Hinton records 56 songs for the Library of Congress.

September: Hank Williams plays the Bostonia Ballroom with Chet Atkins after the Drifting Cowboys are stranded east of the Laguna Mountains by Santa Ana winds; 12-year-old Lou Curtiss is in the crowd (Williams died three months later).

Sam Hinton founds the San Diego Folk Song Society (March 1957); the same year the first beat/folk coffeehouses appear downtown (the Zodiac, under the Pacific Ballroom; the Zen Coffee House and Motorcycle Repair Shop at Broadway and India).
San Diego Folk Song Society founded (Hinton); meets in members' homes.
Kingston Trio forms with San Diego-born Nick Reynolds; John Stewart (also SD-born) joins in 1961.
The Maddox Brothers and Rose own and play the 21 Club in National City (about 1958-59) and briefly a club in Oceanside.

The Upper Cellar coffeehouse (6557 El Cajon Blvd, owner Bob Stane, later of the Ice House and Coffee Gallery) and Circe's Cup near SDSU anchor the Folk Scare era; Harold Darling opens the Sign of the Sun bookstore at Adams and College, which runs San Diego's only regular traditional-music concert series.

Ed Douglas, Larry Murray and Yuris Zeltins open the Blue Guitar music shop (named for a Wallace Stevens poem); Lou Curtiss and Curt Bouterse start a folk song society with weekly jams at San Diego State.

Lou Curtiss and Curt Bouterse start an SDSU branch of the Folk Song Society; coffeehouses of the era include the Upper Cellar (70th & El Cajon), Circe's Cup, the Ballad Man (La Jolla), and the Zen Coffee House and Motorcycle Repair Shop.
Scottsville Squirrel Barkers form around the Blue Guitar store on Midway Drive (1962 per San Diego Troubadour); teen Chris Hillman on mandolin.

Scottsville Squirrel Barkers (Ed Douglas, Larry Murray, Kenny Wertz, Gary Carr, teenage Chris Hillman; later Bernie Leadon) become house band at the Blue Guitar - billed by Douglas as the first bluegrass group in San Diego. Wikipedia dates the band 1961-63; the Troubadour says formed 1962.

Summer: Sign of the Sun concerts taped with Bessie Jones, Jean Ritchie, Jean Redpath, Hedy West, Guy Carawan and Rev. Gary Davis - including what may be the only recording of Davis playing five-string banjo. Mississippi John Hurt, Skip James and the New Lost City Ramblers also played the series (untaped).

Scottsville Squirrel Barkers record their only LP, 'Blue Grass Favorites' (Crown), and disband; Hillman goes on to the Byrds, Leadon to the Eagles, Wertz to the Flying Burrito Brothers and Country Gazette.

Two or three years before 1967, the San Diego Folk Song Society stages a folk festival at Cal Western University on Point Loma with Sam Hinton, Hedy West, the Kentucky Colonels (Clarence and Roland White), Bess Lomax Hawes and Stu Jamieson; in 1964 Hinton hosts a Unitarian Church concert taped by Jack Van Olst.
SDFSS folk festival at Cal Western University, Point Loma (Hedy West, Bess Lomax Hawes, the Kentucky Colonels).

May 11-13: the 1st San Diego State Folk Festival in SDSU's Peterson Gymnasium on a $350 budget - $250 of it for Bill Monroe, backed by Doug Dillard, Dean Webb and Mitch Jayne of the Dillards because his band's bus broke down in El Centro. The festival ran 20 editions through 1987.

July 31: Folk Arts Rare Records opens at 3753 India St. (Washington and India) as festival headquarters, founded by Lou Curtiss with Carol McComb, Gerrie Blake and Stan Smith; Curtiss becomes sole owner within two years.
First San Diego State Folk Festival (Bill Monroe backed by Dillards members); Folk Arts Rare Records opens July 31 at India & Washington.
Lou Curtiss launches the San Diego (State) Folk Festival and opens Folk Arts Rare Records (July 31). Tommy Jarrell, Benny Thomasson and others recorded there through 1975.
Tom Waits works the door at the Heritage coffeehouse, 3842 Mission Blvd (late 1960s, approximate).
San Diego State presents Flatt & Scruggs; 'Cactus Jim' Soldi brings Bill Monroe to the Bostonia Ballroom, El Cajon (late 1960s).
Philippine Fiesta at the Balboa Park Organ Pavilion for San Diego's 200th; about 70 performers.
Ramón 'Chunky' Sánchez arrives at SDSU and joins La Rondalla Amerindia de Aztlán; his 'Chicano Park Samba' becomes the anthem of Chicano Park (founded 1970) and of Chicano Park Day.
Chicano Park takeover (April 22); PASACAT formed; seed of Centro Cultural de la Raza.
Centro Cultural de la Raza inaugurated in Balboa Park (July 11).
Julian banjo & fiddle contest tradition begins (inferred from the 35th annual Julian Bluegrass Festival in 2005); the Balboa Park Old Time Banjo & Fiddle Contests run through the 1970s.

April: Lou Curtiss books Jo-el Sonnier and Doc Guidry at the 6th San Diego Folk Festival, the first Cajun band in San Diego; the same year Curt Bouterse composes the old-time tune 'Waiting for Nancy' in Squibob Square, Old Town.

The Heritage coffeehouse (3842 Mission Blvd, Mission Beach), where Tom Waits had been doorman, closes; on Nov 17, 1973 Waits plays one of the first concerts in the Folk Arts store (about 150 tickets at up to $4), debuting songs that included 'San Diego Serenade'.
San Diego Bluegrass Club founded at Straw Hat Pizza, La Mesa; Julian Banjo & Fiddle Contest begins.
Samahan and the Cupa Cultural Center founded; San Diego Scottish Highland Games incorporated (October).

Tom Waits releases 'The Heart of Saturday Night', including 'San Diego Serenade'; Bob Taylor, Kurt Listug and Steve Schemmer buy the American Dream guitar shop in Lemon Grove, the start of Taylor Guitars.

Dublin uilleann piper Dave Page (b. 1906; Siamsa Gael Céilí Band) retires to San Diego, finds young musicians already running weekly New England-style dances, and becomes the cornerstone of the Irish scene; he revives the Siamsa Gael Céilí Band and plays the 1975 Smithsonian Folklife Festival.
San Diego Scottish Highland Games incorporated.
Taylor Guitars founded (Bob Taylor and Kurt Listug buy the American Dream shop; company now based in El Cajon); San Diego Scottish Highland Games incorporated (October).
Dennis Newsome founds Tekura Jegnas.
Greg and Janet Deering found Deering Banjo Company (Spring Valley).

1970s: about 15 Balboa Park Old Time Banjo and Fiddle Contests (Pepper Grove, then Gold Gulch, crowds of several thousand; $1 entry; prizes of pies, bowling trophies or bags of rutabagas; Byron Berline, Earl Collins and Taj Mahal appeared). Julian's fiddle contests, in contrast, offered cash prizes and grew into the Julian Bluegrass Festival.
Deering Banjo Company founded; RSCDS San Diego branch founded (c.1975, by its 2025 50th anniversary).
Wayne Rice (of Brush Arbor) begins the 'Bluegrass Special' on KSON, which would run 43-44 years.
April: Folk Arts Rare Records moves to 3611 Adams Ave (Normal Heights) after being evicted from 3743 Fifth Ave in Hillcrest; it stays 27 years.
Folk Arts moves to 3611 Adams Ave; Adams Avenue becomes the folk spine of the city.
First San Diego Blues and Black Music Heritage Festival (later editions in 1980 and 1995), staged at Adams Park, which later hosted the Roots Festival.
First San Diego Blues & Black Music Heritage Festival; the Jackstraws chantey band founded.
CCBA Chinese New Year Fair begins downtown.
Moreton Bay Fig Morris founded.
Lou Curtiss starts 'Jazz Roots' on KSDS 88.3 FM (Sunday nights; ran until 2015).
Morava Serbian Folklore Ensemble established at St. George Serbian Orthodox Church.
The San Diego State Folk Festival ends after its 20th edition; the same year San Diego Folk Heritage becomes a nonprofit (it later runs contra dances, concerts and the Sam Hinton festival).
SDSU folk festival discontinued; San Diego Folk Heritage becomes a nonprofit.
San Diego Folk Heritage becomes a nonprofit (per San Diego Troubadour; a filing aggregator says 1979); the San Diego State folk festival is discontinued the same year.
San Diego State folk festival discontinued.
Nickel Creek (Chris Thile, Sara and Sean Watkins, of Vista and North County pizza-parlor bluegrass) forms; it later wins a 2003 Grammy.
Nickel Creek forms out of North County's pizza-parlor bluegrass scene.

February: former tuna fisherman Joe Flammini opens Java Joe's in Poway; Jewel (then a waitress there) launches from its open mic. It moves to Ocean Beach in 1993 and Bacon & Santa Monica in 2000, where Jason Mraz held Thursday nights.
Java Joe's opens in Poway; Jewel, Jason Mraz, Steve Poltz and others come up through its rooms.
Bon Temps Social Club holds its first Cajun dance (Valentine's Day).
Sea Chantey Festival conceived by the Maritime Museum and the Jackstraws, produced with SDFH.
Lou Curtiss starts the free Adams Avenue Roots Festival (some accounts say the first was 1995); the festival numbering continued from the SDSU festivals - the 2002 edition was #29.
Adams Avenue Business Association asks Curtiss to book the Street Fair; the Adams Avenue Roots Festival follows.
Pacific Islander Festival Association founded.
Mariachi enters Sweetwater High curriculum; Mariachi Scholarship Foundation founded by Bob Griego.
Dark Thirty house concerts begin May 3 in Jimmy Duke's Lakeside living room (Joel Rafael Band).
San Diego Bluegrass Club incorporates as the 501(c)(3) San Diego Bluegrass Society.
Rosemary Mantanona founds Guma Imåhen Taotao Tåno', San Diego's first Chamorro dance guma.
Michael Eskin's weekly Ould Sod Irish session begins; Ellen Riley founds San Diego English Country Dancers (October).
ACTA apprenticeship: Jon Meza Cuero teaches Stan Rodriguez the Kumeyaay Wildcat song cycle; LJMS Mariachi Juvenil founded.

September/October: first issue of the San Diego Troubadour (founders Lyle and Ellen Duplessie, Liz Abbott and Kent Johnson) with Lou Curtiss's 'Recordially' column; ACTA pairs Kumeyaay song master Jon Meza Cuero with apprentice Stan Rodriguez to pass on the rare Wildcat song cycle.
First issue of the San Diego Troubadour (September).
May 11: Sam Hinton's last public appearance at the San Diego Folk Heritage Festival in La Jolla, which is permanently renamed the Sam Hinton Folk Heritage Festival (later held at Old Poway Park).
Hinton's last public appearance (May 11) at the SD Folk Heritage Festival, renamed in his honor.

Summergrass bluegrass festival founded by the San Diego Bluegrass Society and the North San Diego County Bluegrass and Folk Club (Antique Gas & Steam Engine Museum, Vista); the Scottsville Squirrel Barkers reunite at the Adams Avenue Roots Festival.
Acoustic Music San Diego begins (Jack Williams at an El Cajon music store); Summergrass founded.
First Summergrass at the Antique Gas & Steam Engine Museum, Vista, after SDBS and NCBFC leave the Julian contest (2002).
Southwestern College launches the world's first mariachi degree; Kumeyaay Community College established; San Diego Taiko formed.

Lou Curtiss wins a $35,128 Grammy Foundation preservation grant; 400 festival reels go to the UCLA Ethnomusicology Archive (collection 2007.04), with digital copies at the Library of Congress. By 2014 more than 860 tapes had been processed.
Jorge Castillo starts Fandango Fronterizo at the border fence.

Jorge Francisco Castillo starts Fandango Fronterizo, an annual son jarocho fandango played on both sides of the border fence at Friendship Park (Border Field State Park / Playas de Tijuana); the same year Curtiss leaves the Roots Festival organization.
First San Diego May Faire Ball (English country dance).
September 10: Sam Hinton dies in Berkeley, aged 92. In spring the Scottsville Squirrel Barkers (Hillman, Wertz, Murray, Douglas, Leadon) reunite at the Adams Avenue Roots Festival.
Julian Family Fiddle Camp inaugurated (CBA).
KPBS reports son jarocho 'thriving' in Tijuana and San Diego, with monthly house fandangos.
The Roots Festival is renamed Adams Avenue Unplugged, with Curtiss back on board.
Adams Avenue Unplugged replaces the Roots Festival; Joel Rafael's Rockin' the Rez starts on Pala's Rez Radio around this time.
Old Time Music / New Expression Music store in North Park closes; Ould Sod session passes its 600th night.
Ramón "Chunky" Sánchez named NEA National Heritage Fellow.
Ramón 'Chunky' Sánchez becomes San Diego's NEA National Heritage Fellow.
June 30: Lou Curtiss closes Folk Arts at 2881 Adams Ave after 47 years and retires; Brendan Boyle reopens the store on El Cajon Blvd on Sept 1.
Lou Curtiss retires; Brendan Boyle takes over Folk Arts Rare Records.
Jazz Roots ends on KSDS; KPRi sold, ending the Homegrown Hour; SDFH presents 20 concerts averaging about 65 people.
Chunky Sánchez dies; Chicano Park designated a National Historic Landmark (Dec 23).
October 28: Chunky Sánchez dies two days before his 65th birthday; about 1,000 mourners attend.
SDFH's San Diego Contra Dance runs weekly (Friday nights) at Trinity United Methodist Church in North Park, 'almost every weekend'.
Comhaltas San Diego (Craobh Barry Cogan) founded, bringing structured Irish music instruction to SD.
Border Patrol stops allowing US-side participation in Fandango Fronterizo; Kumeyaay bird singers open SDSU convocation for the first time.

July 8: Lou Curtiss dies at home in El Cajon/Granite Hills, aged 79 (one Troubadour piece says July 9). The American Folklife Center eulogizes him, and a memorial open mic is held on Nov 18 in the former Bostonia Ballroom.
Lou Curtiss dies (July 8); Java Joe's last location in Old Town becomes the Backdrop.
27th Sea Chantey Festival in the first Festival of the Sea; the Wood 'n' Lips open mic in Santee ends after SESAC licensing demands.

COVID: Summergrass 2020 is cancelled and local bluegrass jams are suspended; in September KSON abruptly cancels Wayne Rice's 44-year Bluegrass Special (it moves to Mountain Country 107.9 FM, Alpine, in December); on Aug 2 the Museum of Man renames itself the Museum of Us.
COVID: the Troubadour goes online-only after losing every advertiser except Folk Heritage; Festival of the Sea postponed indefinitely; AMSD never restarts.
First Indigenous Peoples' Celebration at the Safari Park (San Pasqual Band); Tomcat Courtney dies.
Summergrass returns (Aug 20-22). Vista-raised banjo and fiddle virtuoso Dennis Caplinger (Bluegrass Etc.) dies Aug 14, aged 57.
Dennis Caplinger dies (Aug 14).
Ed Marsh Mariachi Museum opens at Southwestern College.
Post-COVID rebound: 'Live Bluegrass Events are Back'; San Diego Folk Heritage holds 'Loulapalooza', a benefit for a Lou Curtiss documentary (May 14, Carlsbad).
Antique Gas & Steam Engine Museum takes over Summergrass from SDBS/NCBFC.

June 23-25: 'Recordially Yours, Lou Curtiss' (Yale Strom and Elizabeth Schwartz) premieres at the Digital Gym Cinema. The founding nonprofits hand Summergrass to the Antique Gas & Steam Engine Museum, and Carlsbad pipa master Wu Man becomes an NEA National Heritage Fellow.
Songwriter Sanctuary launches (January); Java Joe reunion at SDFH (Jan 8, $30); AMSD founder Carey Driscoll dies (May).

ACTA funds a Fandango Fronterizo apprenticeship program passing son jarocho to Chicano youth in San Diego (a fandango is held in Sherman Heights in March 2024); the Julian Family Fiddle Camp (a CBA event) runs in May.
SD FaSoLa briefly adds a Coronado singing (Feb-Jul).
Comhaltas starts a monthly session at Hooleys, La Mesa; old-time 'North Park Square Dance' series at Verbatim Books reaches its 3rd edition.
Guelaguetza San Diego canceled over immigration enforcement; Keith Ballard retires; House of Somalia opens (Nov); Paul Cuero Jr. dies.
May: Larry Murray (1937-2025), Squirrel Barker and Hearts & Flowers co-founder, dies.
Songwriter Sanctuary becomes a nonprofit; the Troubadour marks its 25th anniversary (Dec 14).
RSCDS San Diego celebrates its 50th anniversary with a ball.
Chula Vista proclaims Kumeyaay People's Day; mariachi museum loses its home; Guelaguetza postponed again; Highland Games move to Mission Valley; HPR 90th; BTSD centennial; 116th Festa.

Living legacy as of 2026: Adams Avenue Unplugged on April 25; Folk Arts Rare Records' Record Store Day on April 18 at 3610 University Ave; Summergrass on Aug 14-16 in Vista; the Troubadour publishes 'Lou Curtiss: The Lost Interview' (July).
Adams Avenue Unplugged (Apr 25, 90+ acts), Sam Hinton festival (Jun 6), Summergrass 24th (Aug), Dark Thirty reunion (Jun 18), Train Song Festival and Tannahill Weavers (Nov).
Balboa Park introduces parking fees; Folk Dance Center prepares to leave Grossmont Center (Bass Pro Shop development); Julian camp renamed Julian Music Camp for 2027.

defunct.name: US-side Fandango Fronterizo at Friendship Park
defunct.why_it_ended: Border Patrol stopped granting permission for the US side after 2018; wall militarization. Festival continues on Tijuana side only.

defunct.name: Chula Vista International Mariachi Festival (bayfront)
defunct.why_it_ended: No evidence after the 8th edition (March 2020) found; possibly a COVID casualty (low confidence).

defunct.name: Ed Marsh Mariachi Museum (public display)
defunct.why_it_ended: Library space agreement ended June 2026; collection in storage pending a new home.

defunct.name: San Diego State Folk Festival
defunct.why_it_ended: SDSU discontinued it after the 20th edition in 1987. Curtiss took five years off and the concept returned on Adams Avenue in 1994. Called by the LOC 'the best traditional music event in the Western United States'.

defunct.name: Adams Avenue Roots Festival
defunct.why_it_ended: Curtiss left the organization in 2008; in 2012 it was rebranded as Adams Avenue Unplugged (still running in 2026, and cancelled in 2020-21 for COVID).

defunct.name: The Heritage coffeehouse (3842 Mission Blvd, Mission Beach)
defunct.why_it_ended: Closed in 1973 (reason not documented). The building later became a yogurt shop and then the Single Fin Surf Bar, which hosted a reunion around 2017. Tom Waits was its doorman.

defunct.name: Sign of the Sun bookstore concert series
defunct.why_it_ended: Owner Harold Darling decided traditional music 'had enough support' and switched to art film (the Unicorn, La Jolla).

defunct.name: The Upper Cellar (6557 El Cajon Blvd)
defunct.why_it_ended: A move to a bigger University Ave site to book name acts failed quickly; owner Bob Stane went to the Ice House in Pasadena.

defunct.name: Circe's Cup (originally La Parise), near SDSU
defunct.why_it_ended: The owner drifted on; it became a pool hall ('Circe's Cue'), then a sandwich shop, and was later demolished for the university.

defunct.name: The Ballad Man (Pearl St, La Jolla)
defunct.why_it_ended: Closed in the early 1960s; no reason given.

defunct.name: The Zodiac and the Zen Coffee House & Motorcycle Repair Shop (downtown)
defunct.why_it_ended: Short-lived; downtown then drew 'sailors on liberty' rather than folk audiences.

defunct.name: Bostonia Ballroom (El Cajon) as a music hall
defunct.why_it_ended: The building survives as the Royal Palace Banquet Hall restaurant; the dance hall is rented for meetings.

defunct.name: 21 Club (National City), owned by the Maddox Brothers and Rose
defunct.why_it_ended: The Maddoxes 'didn't stay club owners too long'.

defunct.name: Balboa Park Old Time Banjo and Fiddle Contests
defunct.why_it_ended: Balboa Park officials stopped providing power for the sound system.

defunct.name: Old Time Cafe (Leucadia/Encinitas)
defunct.kind: listening room (40 seats; owners Bill and Pearl)
defunct.why_it_ended: Closed and later demolished ('by way of the wrecking ball'); exact closing year not found.

defunct.name: Drowsy Maggie's (University Ave, North Park)
defunct.why_it_ended: Not documented. Cindy Lee Berryhill called it 'THE kind of folk venue in the city of San Diego for quite a while' (Rick Saxton's open mic).

defunct.name: In the Alley (Escondido), Bifrost Bridge (La Mesa), Candy Company, Land of Odin, The End
defunct.why_it_ended: All closed by about 1973, leaving 'no place for acoustic music in San Diego', so Folk Arts began store concerts.

defunct.name: Orango's Natural Food Restaurant concert series (Mission Hills)
defunct.why_it_ended: Wound down; concerts moved to the United Methodist Church in 1978.

defunct.name: Java Joe's
defunct.why_it_ended: Moved through Poway, Ocean Beach, Hillcrest, Normal Heights and Old Town (Congress St, 2017). Its domain now hosts unrelated spam, and secondary sources give a 2018 closure (not confirmed).

defunct.name: Amos & Emma Radcliffe house jams
defunct.why_it_ended: Amos died about 2005; Emma moved back to Minnesota about 2009.

defunct.name: Folk Arts Rare Records - Lou Curtiss era
defunct.why_it_ended: Curtiss retired at 75, after being displaced from 3611 Adams by a Curves gym in 2004. The store continues under Brendan Boyle (still open in 2026), so it is not truly defunct.

defunct.name: Jazz Roots (KSDS 88.3)
defunct.why_it_ended: Curtiss retired and his health declined.

defunct.name: Bluegrass Special on KSON
defunct.why_it_ended: KSON's corporate parent cancelled it without notice in Sept 2020; it was revived in Dec 2020 on Mountain Country 107.9 (Alpine).

defunct.name: Mark O'Connor Fiddle Camp, San Diego edition (Point Loma Nazarene University)
defunct.why_it_ended: Reportedly moved when O'Connor left San Diego; dates are uncertain (a teacher's account places SD camps within 2006-2014).

defunct.name: San Diego Blues and Black Music Heritage Festival
defunct.why_it_ended: Sporadic Curtiss production.

defunct.name: Bifrost Bridge (La Mesa), In the Alley (Escondido), the Candy Company, Upper Cellar, Circe's Cup, Ballad Man (La Jolla)
defunct.why_it_ended: The coffeehouse boom passed.

defunct.name: Balboa Park Old Time Banjo & Fiddle Contests
defunct.why_it_ended: Park officials stopped providing power for the sound system.

defunct.name: Julian Banjo & Fiddle Contest / Julian Bluegrass Festival
defunct.why_it_ended: Unknown; no recent editions found (low confidence).

defunct.name: Adams Avenue Roots (& Folk) Festival
defunct.why_it_ended: Rebranded by the business association as Adams Avenue Unplugged in 2012 after Curtiss stepped back.

defunct.name: Acoustic Music San Diego / AMSDconcerts
defunct.why_it_ended: Founder Carey Driscoll's health and the pandemic shutdown; he died in 2023. Troubadour gives the run as 2003-2017 but also says restart talks continued after the pandemic shutdown.

defunct.name: Dark Thirty house concerts (Lakeside)
defunct.why_it_ended: No current schedule found; host Jimmy Duke is in his 90s and is described as the "longtime host" (low confidence).

defunct.name: Wood 'n' Lips Open Mic at Kaffee Meister (Santee)
defunct.why_it_ended: SESAC licensing fees on top of ASCAP/BMI, plus minimum-wage costs.

defunct.name: KSDS "Jazz Roots" (Lou Curtiss)
defunct.why_it_ended: Curtiss retired; he died in 2018.

defunct.name: KPRi 102.1 "Homegrown Hour"
defunct.why_it_ended: Station sold in 2015.

defunct.name: Sea Chantey Festival, Maritime Museum
defunct.why_it_ended: Folded into the Festival of the Sea in 2019; the 2020 edition was postponed indefinitely; no revival found.

defunct.name: Coffeehouses listed as lost: Coffee Cottage, Sweet Delights, Crossroads, Experience Coffee, Bistro Devine, Friendly Grounds, Golden Goose, Rebecca's, South Park Abbey, Bugsy's Brew, Village Emporium, Mikey's
defunct.why_it_ended: Rents, chain competition, wages and licensing.

defunct.name: Weekly San Diego Contra Dance at Trinity United Methodist Church, North Park
defunct.years: c.2010s-2020 (weekly as of Oct 2016 and still described as weekly on a Feb 2021 site snapshot)
defunct.why_it_ended: Not documented; by 2026 SDFH contra is monthly at Liberty Station plus about monthly at Balboa Park Club. Timing suggests the COVID shutdown, but that is an inference.

defunct.name: San Diego Old Time Fiddlers Jam (status unknown)
defunct.why_it_ended: Unknown: only undated listings and a 2013 post found; may continue informally.

defunct.name: Julian Banjo & Fiddle Contest
defunct.why_it_ended: Declining attendance and rotating promoters; became a non-competitive music festival; no current edition found.

defunct.name: SDBS 2nd Tuesday at Fuddruckers (Grossmont / Chula Vista)

tunes_named_for_city.title: Waiting for Nancy
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Composed in 1972 by Curt Bouterse in Squibob Square, Old Town San Diego, while waiting for a friend named Nancy who never came. Now a widespread old-time jam tune: in the Portland Collection (1997), recorded by the Reed Island Rounders, and on the North Atlantic Tune List. Not named for the city, but born there.

tunes_named_for_city.title: Mr and Mrs McLaughlin of San Diego
tunes_named_for_city.tradition: Scottish (reel in G, Scottish country dance music)
tunes_named_for_city.notes: Composed by Muriel A. Johnstone; also filed in a contra collection as 'McLaughlin of San Diego'. Who the McLaughlins were was not found (possibly local Scottish country dance people). | Reel in G by Scottish pianist-composer Muriel Johnstone; also in John Chambers' Contra (KC) collection. Presumably for San Diego Scottish country dancers (connection inferred, not documented).

costs.notes: SDFH contra $15-25 sliding scale (https://sdfolkheritage.org/contradance/); English country dance $10 recorded / $15 live (https://www.sdecd.org/); international folk dance $2-10; RSCDS ~$6/class (12 weeks $70); Pride of Erin ceili $2; modern Western squares ~$5; Cajun/zydeco $10-15. House concerts $25-35 per Jeff Berkley, 2023 (https://sandiegotroubadour.com/house-concerts/); SDFH concerts ~$25-30; Songwriter Sanctuary $10 suggested. Irish and bluegrass jams, Sacred Harp, HPR lawn programs and the Sam Hinton and Train Song festivals are free.

surprises: 'Waiting for Nancy', an old-time jam standard in the Portland Collection, was written in 1972 by San Diego banjo player Curt Bouterse while he waited in Old Town for a friend who never came (https://tunearch.org/wiki/Annotation:Waiting_for_Nancy).

Balboa Park is in effect a city-run folk-dance campus: about 31 modern Western square dance nights a month in central San Diego, plus weekly international, Scottish, céilí, morris and Cajun dancing in city halls, and a free Sunday folk dance open to anyone (https://www.idasdc.com/).

Fandango Fronterizo (2008) plays son jarocho through the border fence at Friendship Park. At the first one, Border Patrol asked them to wrap up, so they played 'La Bamba' for an hour; since 2018 nobody may play on the US side (https://sandiegomagazine.com/everything-sd/arts-culture/fandango-fronterizo-music-festival/).

Southwestern College in Chula Vista began the world's first college music degree with a mariachi specialization in 2004. School mariachi spread in the 1990s partly so Latino parents would come to parent-teacher nights (https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/12/the-one-of-a-kind-mariachi-museum-in-chula-vista-has-lost-its-home-now-what/).

The first San Diego State Folk Festival (1967) had a $350 budget and spent $250 of it on Bill Monroe. The Library of Congress now holds 420 tapes of the 1967-75 festivals, with Tommy Jarrell, Kyle Creed, Benny Thomasson and the Balfa Brothers (https://blogs.loc.gov/folklife/2018/07/lou-curtiss-san-diego-folk-promoter-1939-2018/).

The 1970s Balboa Park Old Time Banjo and Fiddle Contests advertised bribable judges, gave bags of rutabagas as prizes, once split an award between a gospel bluegrass band and Hare Krishna chanters 'for traditional dogma', and ended only when the park stopped supplying electricity (https://sandiegotroubadour.com/fiddle-contests/).

A Navy port that is home to the Star of India has no public shanty sing; the Maritime Museum's Sea Chantey Festival (1993-2019) quietly died with COVID (https://seashanties4all.com/venues/festival-of-sail-in-san-diego/).

San Diego's best folk radio show airs on Rez Radio 91.3, founded by the Pala Band after the 2007 wildfires: Joel Rafael's 'Rockin' the Rez', 449 episodes (https://sandiegotroubadour.com/good-radio-is-out-there-you-just-have-to-know-where-to-look/).

The Comhaltas branch exists because a Cork grandfather, visiting for a christening in 2017, talked the local players into founding one; its founding board member notes she has no Irish heritage (https://www.sandiegocomhaltas.org/comhaltas-in-san-diego-california/).

Kumeyaay bird songs, which singers say were 'hanging from a thread', are now civic protocol: about a dozen bird-singing groups performed at the Safari Park on Indigenous Peoples' Day 2025 (https://www.times-advocate.com/articles/tribe-celebrates-indigenous-peoples-day-at-safari-park/).

Southwestern College in Chula Vista created the world's first college degree with a mariachi specialization in 2004, and its $3.4M mariachi museum (with a Jorge Negrete outfit) went into a storage unit in June 2026: https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/12/the-one-of-a-kind-mariachi-museum-in-chula-vista-has-lost-its-home-now-what/

About a dozen Kumeyaay bird singing groups performed at a single Indigenous Peoples' Day event at the San Diego Zoo Safari Park in 2025, for a song tradition elders describe as once 'hanging from a thread': https://www.times-advocate.com/articles/tribe-celebrates-indigenous-peoples-day-at-safari-park/

At the first Fandango Fronterizo, as Border Patrol asked them to wrap up, musicians launched 'La Bamba' and kept it going for an hour; since 2018 no one has been allowed to answer the verses from the US side: https://sandiegomagazine.com/everything-sd/arts-culture/fandango-fronterizo-music-festival/

San Diego's mariachi-in-schools boom began as a parent-engagement tactic: mariachi on parent-teacher night got immigrant parents into Sweetwater schools: https://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/2026/07/12/the-one-of-a-kind-mariachi-museum-in-chula-vista-has-lost-its-home-now-what/

Point Loma's Portuguese Festa has run since 1910 (116th in 2026), making it the oldest ethnic European religious celebration in San Diego: https://obrag.org/2026/05/portuguese-community-of-point-loma-celebrates-the-116th-festa-do-espirito-santo/

Balboa Park's House of Pacific Relations stages roughly 55 free folk lawn programs a year from 38 cultures, and in Nov 2025 the House of Somalia became its first African house: https://www.sdhpr.org/lp.html

San Diego's Oaxacan Guelaguetza, which ran for about 26 years, was canceled in 2025 and postponed in 2026 because ~40,000 Oaxacans feared immigration enforcement at a public gathering: https://www.kpbs.org/news/border-immigration/2026/10/15/oaxacan-festival-postponed-second-year-in-a-row-because-of-immigration-crackdown

The only NEA National Heritage Fellow based in San Diego County is Chicano songwriter Ramón 'Chunky' Sánchez (2013), who started in SDSU's student rondalla: https://www.arts.gov/honors/heritage/ramon-chunky-sanchez

A Chamorro dance guma practiced for years in the parking lot of SDPD's Southeastern Division station: https://obrag.org/2026/08/one-womans-mission-keeping-the-chamorro-culture-alive-even-after-years-of-colonization-of-their-island-guam/
San Diego Taiko dates only to 2004, not 1969, and 'Soh Daiko' is a New York group, not a San Diego one: https://sandiegotaiko.org/about-3/
The Scottish Highland Games left Vista and in 2026 were held beside Snapdragon Stadium, reachable by trolley: https://sdhighlandgames.org/parking-and-directions/

San Diego's best-known contribution to the old-time jam repertoire, 'Waiting for Nancy', was written in 1972 by Curt Bouterse in Squibob Square in Old Town, while he waited for a Nancy who never showed: https://dulcimerdownloads.com/pages/waiting-for-nancy-history

The first San Diego Folk Festival (May 1967) spent $250 of its $350 budget on Bill Monroe. When his band's bus broke down in El Centro, three Dillards drove down to be his Blue Grass Boys: http://www.folkartsrarerecords.com/library/1st-san-diego-folk-festival/

Folk Arts Rare Records, founded in 1967, outlived its founder: Lou Curtiss sold it in 2014 and it still hosts Record Store Day shows in 2026 at 3610 University Ave: https://www.folkartsrarerecords.com/

The Balboa Park Old Time Banjo and Fiddle Contests (1970s) advertised bribable judges and once awarded one bag of rutabagas for first prize and two bags for second. They ended only because the park stopped supplying electricity: https://sandiegotroubadour.com/fiddle-contests/

Dublin uilleann piper Dave Page, of the 1920s-30s Siamsa Gael Céilí Band, retired to San Diego in 1974 and found weekly New England-style contra dances already running. He became the cornerstone of local Irish music and played the 1975 Smithsonian Folklife Festival: https://www.uilleannobsession.com/article_dave_page

Sam Hinton, the Scripps aquarium curator and marine biologist, founded the San Diego Folk Song Society in 1957 and played all 28 San Diego folk/roots festivals through 2001: https://sandiegotroubadour.com/why-i-love-the-adams-avenue-roots-festival/
Tom Waits got his start as the doorman at the Heritage coffeehouse in Mission Beach; the building is now a surf bar: https://www.sandiegoreader.com/news/2018/jul/09/lou-curtiss-kept-music-alive/
A 1962 tape from the Sign of the Sun bookstore may be the only recording of Rev. Gary Davis playing five-string banjo: https://www.folkartsrarerecords.com/library/

Hank Williams played the Bostonia Ballroom in 1952 with Chet Atkins standing in for the Drifting Cowboys, who were stuck behind Santa Ana winds east of the Laguna Mountains: https://sandiegotroubadour.com/when-hank-williams-came-to-town/

A Scottish reel, 'Mr and Mrs McLaughlin of San Diego' by Muriel Johnstone, is the only fiddle tune found that is literally named for San Diego: https://trillian.mit.edu/~jc/music/abc/by/Muriel_Johnstone/reel/MrAndMrsMcLaughlinOfSanDiego.abc

KSON cancelled Wayne Rice's 44-year Bluegrass Special without notice in Sept 2020, just as IBMA was honoring him; he moved to a low-power station in Alpine: https://sandiegotroubadour.com/the-end-of-an-era-2/

Fandango Fronterizo stages a participatory son jarocho fandango across the border fence at Friendship Park, a rare folk event deliberately played on both sides of an international border: https://actaonline.org/profile/fandango-fronterizo/

The WPA California Folk Music Project (1938-40) apparently recorded nothing in San Diego; a search of the LOC online collection returns zero hits. San Diego's major LOC holdings come instead from Sam Hinton (1947) and Lou Curtiss's tapes: https://lccn.loc.gov/2015655368
Lou Curtiss said San Diego institutions showed no interest in his archive, so it went to UCLA and the Library of Congress instead of SDSU: https://sandiegotroubadour.com/asdf/

Lou Curtiss, the folk-festival impresario, was jailed in 1964 during civil-rights voter registration in Mississippi (per the documentary makers): https://sandiegotroubadour.com/honoring-the-legacy-of-lou-curtiss/

San Diego has no dedicated folk show on any of its terrestrial stations; the steadiest folk program is Joel Rafael's "Rockin' the Rez" on the Pala Band of Mission Indians' Rez Radio, which the Troubadour calls the first indigenous-owned station in Southern California (449 episodes): https://sandiegotroubadour.com/good-radio-is-out-there-you-just-have-to-know-where-to-look/

The 1970s Balboa Park Old Time Banjo & Fiddle Contests had bribable judges, rutabagas as first prize (two bags for second), and once gave a tie award to a gospel bluegrass band and the Hare Krishnas "for traditional dogma": https://sandiegotroubadour.com/fiddle-contests/

The first San Diego State Folk Festival (1967) had a $350 budget and spent $250 of it on Bill Monroe, backed by three of the Dillards because his band had not reached the West Coast: https://sandiegotroubadour.com/a-little-history-of-the-san-diego-folk-festival-and-how-it-got-started/
Tom Waits started as the doorman at the Heritage coffeehouse in Mission Beach; the building is now a surf bar: https://sandiegotroubadour.com/reunion-at-the-heritage/

A local chantey singer learned "Rolling Down to Old Maui" from Stan Hugo, described as the last living chanteyman aboard the tall ships, yet the city's 27-year Sea Chantey Festival seems to have died with COVID: https://sandiegotroubadour.com/the-sea-chantey-festival-a-lifeline-to-our-nautical-past/

Sam Chatmon of the Mississippi Sheiks lived in San Diego from 1966 to 1982 and told Lou Curtiss about his formerly enslaved fiddler father, who played breakdowns like "Old Grey Mule" and "Chickens in the Breadpan Kickin' Up Dough" with whiskers so long he tied them aside: https://sandiegotroubadour.com/sam-chatmon-san-diego-bluesman-talks-with-lou-curtiss/
Two Kingston Trio members, Nick Reynolds and John Stewart, were born in San Diego, and both died there in 2008: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Reynolds

When advertising collapsed around 2020, every San Diego Troubadour advertiser dropped out except San Diego Folk Heritage: https://sandiegotroubadour.com/hey-everybody-the-san-diego-troubadour-is-about-to-celebrate-its-25th-anniversary-and-publisher-liz-abbott-is-here-to-tell-you-about-the-upcoming-celebration-and-fundraiser-along-with-a-bit-about-i/

A Santee open mic was killed by music licensing: SESAC demanded fees about equal to ASCAP and BMI combined, so the coffeehouse banned SESAC songs (Dylan included) and the open mic: https://sandiegotroubadour.com/kiss-open-mics-goodbye/

San Diego Folk Heritage's autumn festival is about trains: songs on the Old Poway Park gazebo while a steam railroad runs rides around the audience: https://sdfolkheritage.org/events/train-song-festival-in-old-poway-park/

Acoustic Music San Diego's founder drew national folk names partly by guilt-tripping his mailing list; Tom Russell said from the stage, "You gotta be drinking to read those emails!": https://sandiegotroubadour.com/carey-driscoll-a-passionate-advocate-for-overlooked-music/

The Library of Congress holds 420 tapes of the first nine San Diego Folk Festivals, with Tommy Jarrell, Seamus Ennis, A.L. Lloyd, Stan Hugill and Bessie Jones among those recorded: https://blogs.loc.gov/folklife/2018/07/lou-curtiss-san-diego-folk-promoter-1939-2018/

Java Joe's moved roughly ten times in 27 years (Poway, two Ocean Beach rooms, Hillcrest, Mission Valley, a North Park temple, a downtown hotel, a pub, Normal Heights, Old Town): https://www.sandiegoreader.com/news/2018/oct/18/say-goodbye-java-joes/

Contra shrank by more than half: in 2016 San Diego Contra danced weekly (Fridays) at Trinity United Methodist Church in North Park, and the site still said 'each week' in Feb 2021; in 2026 SDFH runs one monthly dance at Liberty Station plus roughly one Balboa Park Wednesday. http://web.archive.org/web/20161006091556id_/http://sandiegocontra.org/ and https://sdfolkheritage.org/contradance/

A metro of 3.3 million has exactly one weekly Irish pub session (The Ould Sod, every Tuesday since 2000, seats for 6-8 players), and The Session lists only three SD sessions in total. https://thesession.org/sessions/759

San Diego had no Comhaltas branch, and almost no structured Irish music instruction, until 2017, when a visiting Corkman, Barry Cogan, talked session players into founding one at his grandson's christening. Its founding board member Judy Carlstrom notes she has no Irish heritage. https://www.sandiegocomhaltas.org/comhaltas-in-san-diego-california/

Balboa Park is a city-run folk-dance campus: international folk dance Mon/Tue/Wed nights and a FREE Sunday 12:30-4 dance at the Balboa Park Club, square dance clubs most nights in the Recital Hall and War Memorial Building, céilí and Scottish country classes in the Casa del Prado, and morris practice on Tuesdays, mostly at $2-$7 a night under the Parks & Rec-backed International Dance Association. https://www.idasdc.com/intl-folk-clubs

Modern Western square dancing out-schedules every 'trad' form: about 31 club nights a month in central San Diego alone (seven weekly clubs), against about 2 contra dances. https://www.sdsda.org/get_dates.asp

Two of the world's biggest acoustic instrument makers are East County neighbors: Taylor Guitars (El Cajon, 1974) and Deering Banjos (Spring Valley, 1975; North America's largest banjo maker). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deering_Banjo_Company

San Diego's bluegrass club was founded in 1973 in a Straw Hat Pizza in La Mesa with $2 lifetime dues, and pizza parlors remain the jam venue of choice: Round Table Pizza hosts three jam nights (NCBFC's 1st Tuesday and 3rd Wednesday in Escondido, plus the weekly Thursday Night Pickers in Encinitas), and Nickel Creek's members grew up playing SD pizza joints as 'Seldom Clean'. https://www.sandiegobluegrass.org/PDFs/History-of-SDBS%20lr.pdf

A Midway Drive guitar shop with a partial dirt floor, the Blue Guitar, had a house band (the Scottsville Squirrel Barkers) that launched a Byrd (Chris Hillman), an Eagle (Bernie Leadon) and a Flying Burrito Brother (Kenny Wertz). http://bcbrown.net/bluegrass/chronicles/articles/ICMC2007/SSB_paper.pdf

Lou Curtiss's San Diego State Folk Festival (1967-75 tapes now at the Library of Congress) recorded Tommy Jarrell, Kyle Creed, Benny Thomasson, Kenny Hall, Earl Collins, Louis Boudreault and the Balfa Brothers. San Diego was a stop for the great tradition-bearer fiddlers long before it had an old-time jam scene. https://blogs.loc.gov/folklife/2018/07/lou-curtiss-san-diego-folk-promoter-1939-2018/

Old-time is the weakest link for a visiting fiddler: no verifiable 2024-26 old-time jam was found (the 'San Diego Old Time Fiddlers Jam' trail goes cold in 2013), there is no CSOTFA district in the county, and the 1973 Julian Banjo & Fiddle Contest is gone. Meanwhile a young stringband scene runs ticketed 'North Park Square Dance' nights in a used bookstore. https://clintonrossdavis.com/3rd-ever-north-park-square-dance/

The Folk Dance Center, SD's dedicated international folk dance hall at Grossmont Center, is being evicted by a Bass Pro Shop; its goodbye party, with the Balkan band Tzidia, is Dec 19, 2026, months before it hosts the 2027 statewide folk dance festival in Balboa Park. http://folkdancecenter.org/newsletter.html

San Diego's English country dancers mostly dance to recorded music ($10) on Sunday afternoons at a Rancho Bernardo tennis club. The group's founder practiced figures at home with towels spread on the floor as partners before she found anyone to dance with. https://www.sdecd.org/about.html

Rare named tune: 'Mr and Mrs McLaughlin of San Diego', a reel by Scottish composer Muriel Johnstone, is the only tune with a San Diego title found in the indexes searched (abcnotation/John Chambers' collection). https://trillian.mit.edu/~jc/music/abc/by/Muriel_Johnstone/reel/MrAndMrsMcLaughlinOfSanDiego.abc

Bluegrass jams have moved from pizza parlors and Fuddruckers to craft breweries: three monthly jams now run at Duck Foot Brewing taprooms (Miramar and Leucadia). https://northcountybluegrass.org/camping/

The SDBS slow jam schedule disagrees with itself across the two clubs' websites (4th Tuesday at Mission Valley Library on SDBS; 3rd Monday at varying locations on NCBFC). https://www.sandiegobluegrass.org/events.html
curiosities: Do metros with city-owned dance halls (San Diego's Balboa Park, run with Parks & Rec) keep more weekly folk dancing than metros that depend on churches and private venues?
San Diego's contra went from weekly (2016-2021) to about twice a month while its square dance and international clubs held up. Is contra the most COVID-fragile folk dance nationally, and why?
Why do some cities with deep old-time histories (San Diego: Bouterse, the festival tapes, Clinton Davis) have no regular old-time jam? What makes old-time jams take root?
Which metros' Irish scenes rest on a Comhaltas branch, and when did each branch arrive? San Diego's dates only from 2017; SF's from the early 1970s.
How do border metros (San Diego-Tijuana, El Paso, Laredo) practice cross-border folk traditions, and how has 2025-26 immigration enforcement affected heritage festivals such as Guelaguetza?
Military migration seeds folk traditions: Navy-linked Filipino and Chamorro troupes in San Diego, Appalachian-born retirees in its bluegrass. Does the same hold in Norfolk, San Antonio or Tampa?
Where did Sam Hinton-style 'folk song society' clubs (SF 1948, San Diego 1957) survive, and what replaced them where they faded?

How many US school districts besides Sweetwater Union have curricular mariachi at middle-school level, and which metro has the most student mariachi players per capita (San Diego vs. Tucson, San Antonio, LA)?

Are there other places where an Indigenous song tradition (Kumeyaay bird songs) is now routinely used as civic protocol (university convocations, city proclamations), and has that increased the number of active singers?
Which other heritage festivals in US border or immigrant-heavy metros were canceled or postponed in 2025-26 over immigration enforcement, and is there a pattern by tradition?

Does any other city have a standing multi-ethnic folk-dance stage like Balboa Park's House of Pacific Relations lawn programs (90 years, ~55 programs/year), and how does its audience compare to international folk dance clubs?
How do the Point Loma Portuguese Festa (1910) and Holy Ghost festas in the Bay Area, Central Valley, New England and Hawaii compare in age, size and continuity?
How does the Navy shape folk scenes: are Filipino and Chamorro dance groups similarly strong in Norfolk, Bremerton/Kitsap, Pensacola and Honolulu?
Why has son jarocho stayed a transborder phenomenon in San Diego (centered in Tijuana) while LA and the Bay Area developed large US-side fandango networks?
How many NEA Heritage Fellows per million residents does each of the 20 metros have, and why does San Diego have only one?
Which metros have tribal community colleges or tribally run cultural centers that teach song traditions, and does that correlate with powwow/song vitality?
Is blues as a community practice (house parties, jams, elders) dying in West Coast metros like San Diego faster than in Southern or Midwestern ones?

Several big metros had a record-store-plus-festival hub like Folk Arts / San Diego State Folk Festival (e.g. McCabe's in LA, Folklore Center in NYC, Fret Shop in Chicago?). Which survived their founders, and why did Folk Arts?
San Diego's college folk festival (SDSU 1967-87) died in 1987 while others continued. Do university-run folk festivals in other metros show the same 1980s die-off?

Is San Diego's unusually dense bluegrass scene (20+ bands, a jam most days, attributed to military retirees from Appalachia) matched in other Navy/military towns such as Norfolk, Jacksonville, Tacoma and San Antonio?
How many other metros have a widely played old-time tune composed locally (like 'Waiting for Nancy')? Is there a pattern of 1970s California revivalists writing tunes that became jam standards?
Which metros' 1960s-70s coffeehouse and festival tape archives have been digitized (Curtiss at UCLA/LOC), and which were lost? Is there a cross-city inventory?
The WPA California project skipped San Diego. Did other Sun Belt metros (Phoenix, Tampa, Orlando, Miami) also miss 1930s federal folk documentation?
Cross-border folk events (Fandango Fronterizo) - do El Paso/Juárez or Detroit/Windsor have equivalent participatory traditions played across the line?
Kumeyaay bird-song revival vs. other Native song revivals in big metros (e.g. Gabrielino-Tongva in LA, Ohlone in SF): which have institutional support such as ACTA apprenticeships or tribal museums?
When did contra dancing start in each metro? San Diego had weekly New England-style dances by 1974 - earlier than many Sun Belt cities?
Do other cities have a long-running local acoustic-music print magazine like the San Diego Troubadour (2001-present), and does having one correlate with better-documented scene history?

Folk song societies founded in the 1950s (San Diego's in 1957): how many still exist in the 20 metros, and how many have shrunk, as San Diego's has, from four meetings a month to one library song circle?
Have Nashville-style "writers rounds" replaced folk song circles and open mics as the main participatory singing format in other cities since COVID?

Which port cities' maritime museums kept public chantey festivals or monthly shanty sings going after COVID (Mystic, SF Maritime, Seattle, Baltimore), and why did San Diego's lapse despite the 2021 TikTok shanty boom?
How many of the 20 metros have no terrestrial folk radio show at all? Is a tribal or community station the main folk outlet anywhere else?
Did PRO licensing (especially SESAC since about 2015) measurably shrink coffeehouse open mics nationally, or only in some states?
Shape-note density: San Diego has about 3 singings a month for 3.3M people and no annual singing of its own. How does that compare per capita, and which metros host their own all-day singings?
How many metros' folk festivals were founded by a record-store owner (Lou Curtiss/Folk Arts), and do those outlast university-sponsored ones?
Is one church acting as a decades-long folk hub (Normal Heights United here) a common pattern, and which other congregations play that role?
Do storytelling guilds formally share an organization with folk-music and contra societies elsewhere, as at San Diego Folk Heritage?
House-concert series that ended with their founders (Dark Thirty, AMSD): is the house-concert circuit shrinking nationally as its 1990s-era hosts age out?
Are free neighborhood "walkabout" festivals (Adams Avenue Unplugged) replacing curated folk festivals in other metros?

Did contra dance in other Sun Belt metros (Phoenix, Houston, Dallas, Orlando) also shrink from weekly to monthly after COVID, or is San Diego's drop to about 2 a month unusual? What explains it: venues, callers, or the musician pool?

Why does San Diego, with a large Irish-American population and the biggest St. Patrick's parade 'west of the Mississippi' (per Comhaltas SD), support only one weekly pub session, while smaller metros (Seattle, Denver) support many?
How many metros have a city-parks-backed umbrella like IDASDC that keeps folk dancing at $2 a night in municipal buildings, and does subsidized space predict folk-dance longevity?
Is modern Western square dancing larger than contra in nights per month in most US metros, as it is in San Diego (about 31 vs about 2)?
Where do the instrument-making hubs (Taylor/Deering in SD; Gibson/Nashville; Martin/Nazareth) sit relative to each city's actual jam density? Does local manufacturing feed local scenes?
Has pizza-parlor bluegrass (Straw Hat, Round Table, Shakey's, Fuddruckers) given way to breweries in other Western metros too, and does the venue shift change who shows up?
Which metros lack a CSOTFA/state old-time fiddlers' district or a fiddle contest, and is that associated with a weak old-time jam scene?
